title: What If We Had Time?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. reflects on catching himself running bedtime with his four children on the same rushed, efficiency-minded autopilot he uses at work, and what changed when he asked, "What if I pretended I had all the time in the world for this?" He walks through each child individually - his five-year-old son, eight-year-old daughter, ten-year-old daughter, and twelve-year-old daughter - describing what each one actually wants from him at bedtime, from brief affirmation to extended snuggling to simply being asked good questions. The surprising finding is that slowing down and being fully present cost him almost no extra time overall, while transforming the emotional quality of the ritual and his relationship with each child. He closes by naming the broader lesson: habits that serve him well professionally, like efficiency, can be quietly corrosive at home, where presence rather than speed is the actual currency.
points: Names a specific, transferable failure mode: bringing workplace efficiency habits into a home context where they are "foolish" rather than helpful.
Demonstrates that slowing down at bedtime cost almost no extra total time, undercutting the assumption that presence and efficiency are always in tension.

Individually profiles what each of four children (ages five, eight, ten, twelve) actually wants from a parent at bedtime, modeling attentive, child-specific parenting rather than a one-size-fits-all routine.
Reframes his twelve-year-old's desire to "teach him how to be the dad of a teenager" as a gift rather than a nuisance, modeling humility toward an aging parent-child relationship.
quotes: A few weeks ago, I had an epiphany: what if, instead of rushing bedtime with my kids, I pretended that I had enough time to give them the love they each desired?
I was bringing my daytime efficiency to this nighttime ritual - night after night, week after week.
She never gets tired of me telling her that I love her and how special she is. She's incredibly attentive to the degree to which I'm relaxed with her.

She also wants to teach me how to be the dad of a teenager - that's been a major blessing of an insight for me, that she doesn't want to find me annoying and out of touch and clueless (haha, it's true!)

I share this with you, colleague, because sometimes habits that are smart and wise at work - habits like aiming toward efficiency, like building relationships via tracked MGCs - are actually foolish at home.
Hey Dave - what if you actually did have all the time in the world for this?
